title: Q10: The Jagged Frontier
subtitle: Why 'simple' is a human notion the model never learned
author: DLS 2026 — Kukla
notes: Companion video V2 spec per paradise 2026-10-10. Each segment carries a 'visual' field: 'slide' = PIL text+bullets (existing working path), 'manim' = named Manim scene class to render + mux. slide.title: The Jagged Frontier
slide.subtitle: Why models ace relativity but miscount letters in 'strawberry'

segments.narration: Large language models can explain general relativity, then turn around and miscount the letters in the word strawberry. This module is about why that happens — and why it is predictable, not random.

slide.title: The puzzle
bullets: Student question #18: why solve complex problems yet make simple mistakes?
This is a shape of competence, not a bug to patch away

segments.narration: Here is the puzzle a student raised. The same system that handles complex reasoning fails at tasks a child finds trivial. The key insight: this uneven shape of competence tells us something real about how these models work.

segments.manim_note: Animated contrast: a smooth human competence curve (hard implies easy follows) vs a jagged model curve with sharp unpredictable spikes/dips across task-difficulty axis. Highlight that 'hard' and 'easy' are human axis labels the model never optimized for. Course palette; curve draws left-to-right with run_time ~6s, then jagged overlay reveals.
segments.narration: For humans, competence is correlated: if you can do the hard version, the easy version follows. For models it is a jagged frontier — sharp, unpredictable variation across tasks. The reason is that hard and easy are human notions the model never learned.

slide.title: Root cause 1: the training objective
bullets: Trained to predict the next token, not to be uniformly competent
Capability tracks training frequency, not logical difficulty
Relativity prose is abundant; exact long arithmetic is rare

segments.narration: First root cause: the training objective. A model is trained to predict the next token, not to be uniformly good at everything. So its capability tracks how often a pattern appeared in training, not how logically hard it is. Relativity prose is everywhere online; exact long arithmetic is comparatively rare.

segments.manim_note: Core motion diagram. Show the word 'strawberry' as contiguous letters, then animate the BPE split into sub-word token boxes (e.g. 'straw' | 'berry' or real tokenizer chunks) sliding apart. Then pose 'count the r's' and show the letter-level structure is gone inside the opaque token boxes. Opacity-layer the letters fading behind the token boxes. run_time table: letters 2s, split 3s, query overlay 2s, letters-gone reveal 3s.
segments.narration: Second root cause: tokenization. The model never sees individual letters. It sees sub-word tokens — chunks like straw and berry. Counting the r's in strawberry requires letter-level structure that simply is not represented inside those token boxes. The same fragmentation breaks positional arithmetic on long numbers.

slide.title: Root cause 3: one forward pass
bullets: One forward pass — no scratchpad, no built-in verification
Humans re-check; a base model doesn't unless prompted or given a tool
Often fixed instantly by 'think step by step'

segments.narration: Third root cause: a base model answers in a single forward pass with no scratchpad and no built-in verification. Humans re-check their work; the model does not, unless you prompt it to or give it a tool. That is why the same model often fixes the error the instant you say: think step by step.

slide.title: Predicting the jaggedness
bullets: Weak where: exact symbols, long chains, sub-token info, rare knowledge
Fix: pair brittle regimes with reasoning, tools, and verifiers

segments.narration: Putting it together gives a predictive heuristic. Models are strong where tasks are well-represented, error-tolerant, and pattern-like; weak where they need exact symbols, long reasoning chains, sub-token information, or rare knowledge. The practical fix is to pair the brittle regimes with explicit reasoning, external tools, and verifiers.

slide.title: Takeaway
slide.subtitle: The frontier is jagged by construction — design around it, don't be surprised by it

segments.narration: The takeaway: the capability frontier is jagged by construction, a direct consequence of the objective, tokenization, and single-pass inference. Once you expect it, you can design around it instead of being surprised by it.
